en: The Sūtra on the Meaning of Non-Self in the Noble Mahāyāna Dharma as Questioned by the Tīrthikas,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu,
Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Dharma-Preaching Master, Your Servant.
Translated by Fātian by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was in the midst of a great assembly. At that time, there were non-Buddhists who harbored doubts they wished to resolve; being confused regarding the practice of the Mahāyāna, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with profound reverence, joined their ten fingers in palms-together salutation, and asked about the meaning of non-self:
"Great Man, you are the All-Knowing One, and you constantly teach that this body is without self."
If the body is without self and its intrinsic nature is also non-existent, how can there be such things as lamentation and weeping, laughter and play, hatred and love, or double-tongued speech?
From what would these arise?
This is what I doubt; I pray that you will grant me its resolution.
Regarding what the Tathāgata has spoken concerning the body and its fundamental nature—how do existence and non-existence relate?
The Buddha said, "O outsider!
Listen attentively and receive this well; I shall explain it for you."
The Buddha said:
"Because the body and its fundamental nature are essentially empty in substance, to speak of them as either 'existent' or 'non-existent' constitutes two dharmas;
to say that they exist is itself further delusion."
The Buddha said:

"One should contemplate the entire body—from the hair, nails, skin, and body hair, to the two hands, the pair of feet, and even down to the fat, tendons, spleen, intestines, marrow, and bones—pervading both the interior and exterior, yet not perceiving an inherent nature."
The non-Buddhist said:
“Great Being! If he does not see his own fundamental nature, how could I, with my physical eyes, possibly see it?”
"Or can one see it with the divine eye?
The Buddha said:
"When the divine eye sees that, it is without form, without marks, and without abiding; this seeing is not seeing."
The non-Buddhists said:
"If you speak thus, the Great Sage speaks falsely.
If those [states] do not exist, why is it that we clearly perceive these occurrences of weeping and laughing, frolicking, anger, hatred and love, and double-tongued speech?"
Because this is so, how can it be said that [things] do not exist?
Furthermore, to say that they "either exist or do not exist" establishes two distinct meanings. He also said:
“Great Being! If it cannot be said whether that [object] exists or does not exist, how can you say that he has an attachment or that he has no attachment?
He further said:
"What is the destination of emptiness?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
"Emptiness is not that which is reached, for its essence cannot be apprehended.
The non-Buddhist said:
"If this is so, then regarding matters such as laughing and weeping, frolicking, anger, hatred and love, and double-tongued speech—what would be seen?"
The Buddha said:
"It is like a dream, like an illusion, like a transformation, like a reflected image.
The non-Buddhist said:
"What is the characteristic of a dream?
What is the characteristic of a magical illusion?
What is the characteristic of a reflected image?"
The Buddha said:
"Illusions have no marks; emptiness is not something to be grasped; dreams are empty in their very essence.
Because they are like a mirage, reflections have no color; they are false and unreal."
All that is seen, up to and including all phenomena, should be viewed as being like an illusion, like a magical transformation, like a dream, and like a shadow.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of vision that adorn suchness.
That which is adorned is designated as "self" and that which is not is designated as "other.
This is called a person (*pudgala*), and this is called the worldly conceptualization of a person.
As for wealth, sons and daughters, brothers, wives and concubines, and so forth, these are called the adornments contemplated by the mind.

Such phenomena as these have no self and no other; they have no person and no life-force; they have no *pudgala*, no sentient being, no world, no seer, no wealth, no sons or daughters, no friends, and no wives or concubines.
Since all those phenomena do not possess intrinsic nature, how can there be that supramundane adornment of karmic fruition, or the arising and ceasing of good and evil?
That adornment of fruition within True Suchness is neither good nor evil, neither arising nor ceasing, and possesses neither affliction nor bliss; yet all these dharmas are each exactly like this!

Furthermore, there are two kinds of adornment—mundane and supramundane—which cause sentient beings, by virtue of these adornments, to give rise to afflictions and remain in saṃsāra, circling for a long time without knowing True Suchness (tathatā).

Those who know the Dharma contemplate its adornment, yet they harbor doubts regarding this suffering sensation; because they perceive that suffering sensation as evil, they distance themselves from liberation and fail to see the Path.

Due to their deluded attachments, ignorant sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death and fall into the miserable realms; practicing worldly dharmas, they do not perceive True Suchness (tathatā). As their saṃsāra comes to an end, it is like weaving a web with thread—moving back and forth in succession.
"Furthermore, just as the two luminaries, the sun and the moon, travel through the world, appearing and disappearing, emerging and setting, day and night;

so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) impermanent and soon destroyed, and their revolving through birth and death, coming and going, is likewise. Yet the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is free from such descriptive phrases."
Furthermore, those gods, gandharvas, and their consorts who dwell in the heavens fall into all states of existence due to the retribution of their adornments;

likewise, there are vidyādhara-attainers, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas who, through the retribution of all their adornments, fall into hell; and the gods of "Evil Diligence" (Duḥśīla), who perform meritorious deeds through their supernatural powers, may fall into those very heavens by virtue of the retribution of all their adornments.

"Furthermore, even if one were Śakra or a Wheel-Turning King, possessing the most supreme virtues and the most supreme status, and were endowed with all such fruits of adornment, they might still be reborn among the animals."

At all times, the wise person should appropriately distance themselves from the supreme great bliss of the heavens and constantly contemplate the bodhicitta—vividly luminous and expansive, devoid of intrinsic nature, free from obstruction, and without abiding; all things are empty, and one should likewise remain far removed from all conceptual proliferation.
“O non-Buddhists!
The characteristics of the bodhicitta are neither hard nor soft, neither hot nor cold; it is without tactile sensation and without grasping.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the bodhicitta are neither long nor short, neither round nor square, neither fat nor thin.”
Furthermore, the characteristic of the bodhicitta is neither white nor black, neither red nor yellow; it is neither color nor characteristic.

That bodhicitta does not produce characteristics and is not manifest; it is without intrinsic nature and without entanglement. Because it is like space and devoid of color, the characteristic of the bodhicitta is beyond observation.
"O outsider!
It is because you do not know that the characteristic of the bodhicitta is in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the bodhicitta is pure by nature; it is without substance, beyond analogy, and cannot be seen—it is the supreme expression."

Furthermore, the characteristic of the bodhicitta is not any material form; it has no counterpart. It is like water forming bubbles: though they are seen, they do not exist. It is like the metaphors of magical illusions and mirages, or like a lump of clay fashioned into various vessels; though all their names are present, they are entirely mere conceptual proliferation.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth also exist as illusory transformations, for they are of one taste with emptiness; like lightning, they do not remain perceptible for even a single moment.
Contemplating that Prajñāpāramitā and performing various virtuous deeds is likewise thus!
As for laughter, jesting, play, song, dance, joy, food, drink, and sensual desires—all are like a dream.

Since the essential nature of the conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) of sentient beings is ultimately empty and the mind is like space, how could doubt possibly arise? One should thus practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If one constantly contemplates in this manner and realizes the nature of all things, one will naturally attain liberation and reach the supreme state.
The unsurpassed Bodhi spoken of by all Buddhas arises from this; one should practice such contemplation.

One who practices this contemplation attains the supreme nirvāṇa; even all transgressions committed in the past are entirely extinguished, and immeasurable virtues arise. Thus, in this very life, one remains unstained by faults, and through dedicated application to the practice of contemplation, definitive accomplishment is attained.

If one is not in accord with True Suchness (tathatā), one should recite the mantra of non-True Suchness and the seal of the non-arising of True Suchness associated with the vajra-bell, and then give rise to conduct that accords with True Suchness, whereby one will certainly perfect the aforementioned merits.

At that time, having heard these words, the non-Buddhists examined them with careful scrutiny, and all the snares of their doubt were completely severed. Having made this observation, they attained abiding in the Mahāyāna; looking up in joyful veneration, they paid homage and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Meaning of Non-Self in the Mahāyāna Asked by Non-Buddhists about the Noble Ones.
